item.description:
You can smell it in the air can't you? The chill in your nostrils and the earthy whiff as leaves fall and the sun departs for another year. Yes, autumn is here, meaning we're teetering on the cavernous hole of near-nothingness as the entire games industry gives GTA 6 the widest berth imaginable. But that doesn't mean there isn't stuff to be excited about, of course. And the latest edition of the Galaxies Showcase has chucked a few more things onto the 'ooooh intriguing!' pile. Actually, quite a lot of things given its nearly two-hour runtime; but while you can watch the full thing in its entirety if you've got the time, we've also picked out a few of the announcements that especially caught our eyes and highlighted them below. Was all this really just an excuse for Connor to enthuse about penguins? Perhaps!
I've been very excited about Bristol developer Friday Sundae's There are no Ghosts at the Grand ever since I saw it at a preview last year. It's one of those things that reads like a checklist of my very specific gaming interests, being part musical, part home renovation sim, and part ghostbusting mystery adventure, all unfolding in a dilapidated hotel in a British seaside town.
The idea is you've got 30 days to renovate it (exactly why is part of the mystery given its protagonist has motives so secret, he'll even try hiding them from the player), but there's plenty more to do besides: you can explore the cobblestone streets, go sailing out at sea, or take a scooter into the countryside as you attempt to uncover the truth about the hotel's strange past. By night, there are ghosts to deal with - and throughout all this, the cast is prone to bursting into song. And if that tickles your fancy in the same way it's tickling mine, you can play a Steam demo right now ahead of its December arrival.
AfterZero: The Last Drive is possibly the first Pacific Drive-like, in that it's a game about driving a car across a post-apocalyptic wasteland - where you'll scavenge, fix up, and upgrade your car, and build out your hideout. It's the work of 3DClouds, the studio mostly known for Formula Legends, but The Last Drive is an altogether different beast. There's a focus on environmental and traversal challenges, similar to the Snow/MudRunner games, or Over the Hill more recently. Its setting caught my eye, too, unfolding in a post-industrial world where it's always winter. Everything is covered in snow, and the reveal trailer hints there's a mystery at the heart of it all. Like Formula Legends, The Last Drive has a sort of blocky, inky artstyle that elevates its plastic toy-looking cars and objects, and it's releasing sometime in 2027 for PC (Steam), PS5, and Xbox Series X/S.
Contact Protocol is an eerie, grim-looking (in a good way) starship job sim that places you in the shoes of a security officer working for a greedy corporation. Your decisions, while surely horrid, are keeping a crew of miners alive as you set course for Jupiter's biggest moon. Aside from a killer premise, Contact Protocol has a wonderful aesthetic, offering a dirty, grisly look - full of delicious retro hardware - at a ruthless life among the stars. There's a demo available on Steam now, and the full game's out next year.
It's hard to explain why, but Late Shift immediately reminded me of Susanna Clarke's wonderful story Piranesi. I think it's to do with the game being about escaping from a world you find yourself trapped in. Maybe it's also just because there's a section with a white hallway.
On closer inspection, Late Shift, from developer AstroCat Studios, is probably more like Remedy's work, presenting players with a bizarre, incoherent world that they have to find their way out of. Specifically, it's a "short found-footage anomaly horror game", according to the Late Shift Steam page, told through the eyes of a missing cinema employee. Did you know former Eurogamer people Tom Phillips and Martin Robinson both used to work at cinemas? Perhaps it's their story Late Shift brings to life. The trailer announced the release of a Late Shift demo, and the full game is "coming soon".
Call me superficial, but I was onboard with Deperson the second I saw its artstyle. Developer Error Thing describes its game as a "self-reflective psychological horror adventure", and that begins when protagonist Aaron mysteriously finds himself in Indrija, a "nation consumed by surveillance and fear". I'm not entirely sure what genre we're dabbling with here on the gameplay front, but it's got an air of point-and-click puzzler to it and it sounds like there might be a bit of action too. "Sometimes you'll need to run. Sometimes you'll need to think carefully," says Error Thing. "Deperson is not a forgiving game." Whatever it is, though, it's certainly a looker, with a wonderfully unnerving hand-drawn animation style that's as surreal as it is striking. Deperson is set to launch sometime next year, but there's a demo out now on Steam, so I guess I know what I'm doing this weekend.
I had no idea about When Sirens Fall Silent until last night, but it stood out like a fart in a church during the Galaxies Showcase. This heavy psychological serial killer horror is the new game from Martha is Dead and Town of Light studio LKA, and I'm in love with the mood and styling of it. That's an odd thing to say given the subject matter, but its story appears to be told through a mixture of news reports, recorded interviews, and various pieces of media, all painstakingly styled with a mid-90s aesthetic. The result is something not unlike a true crime documentary, and I'm very fond of those.
The part I'm worried about, after seeing a pretty young woman in a plunging neckline top manacled to a chair in the opening, is that there's a questionably seedy undertone to the trailer. But reading more about When Sirens Fall Silent reveals it to be a story directly dealing with misogyny, trafficking, trauma, and - much more hopefully - redemption. It's got me fascinated, and it's due next year.
Now, in itself, a Knight Rider crossover trailer for Stuntman: Hollywood - a game already bulbous with Universal IP crossovers, ranging from Jurassic World and Miami Vice to Back to the Future - isn't especially exciting. But it has reminded me of my very tired, very confused time with it at this year's Gamescom. The gist is you, a stunt man, race around circuits as a bullish director bellows instructions at you in a bid to get the perfect shot.
That might be a daredevil hairpin bend on a freeway, or a race against a speedboat, or - in the case of the Jurassic World stage I played - an absolutely wild motorbike chase while a volcano erupts and dinosaurs pursue you. It's a game that demands pretty quick reactions, which is exactly what I didn't have as the show was drawing to a close and my Gamescom flu was setting in - and I was terrible. But I did enjoy the ridiculous spectacle of it all, and its Galaxies Showcase trailer has reminded me it's one to keep an eye on.
Kingdom is the game series that comes to mind when I see Wild n Chill. Because, just as Kingdom did fantasy town-building side-on and in pixel art, Wild n Chill is doing survival games in the same way. The vibes, as no one says, are immaculate: a person and their dog go out into the wilderness and set about chopping down trees and constructing a shelter and then building a solitary life out there. It's cosy, it's warming, it's peaceful.
I just wish you didn't have to be so crude as to chop down trees. It's a personal bugbear of mine, but you wouldn't presume to go out into the wilderness and start chopping down trees in real life, would you? You're overthinking it, Bertie. You're overthinking it. Wild n Chill is "coming soon" to PC (Steam) and now all of the consoles, by the looks of it. The brilliantly named Wombat Brawler is making it - a team that's made a few similar other games before.
Mr. Records immediately caught my eye when it showed up during Day of the Devs earlier this year. It's the latest game from Glee Cheese, the studio that made the enjoyable A Musical Story back in 2022, and tells the tale of a man named George who can travel through music. As he does, players are transported through vibrant worlds they'll need to rhythmically interact with. There seems to be a bit of a management focus too, given that each level, when completed, turns into a vinyl LP you'll need to match with customers back in your record store, and it all looks delightful. What's more, we now know it'll feature a level editor when it comes to PC in Q2 next year. Oh, and there's a Steam demo too.
One of the most surprising reveals at Galaxies was that Squad is coming to PS5 and Xbox Series X/S in 2027. Squad, if you don't know, is essentially a more approachable version of Arma, in that it's a realistic multiplayer shooter where class dependency and logistical planning are core elements of gameplay. Matches in Squad feature combined arms combat and take place across massive maps - up to 4x4km and supporting 100 players.
Squad on console, which doesn't yet have a release date, includes select maps from the PC version and it also supports console cross-play. But if you've ever seen gameplay of Squad, you'll know it seems nearly impossible to translate that depth - especially in UI and command options - to controllers, but the developers at Offworld Industries believe they've figured it out. They're so confident, in fact, there's an PS5 Alpha Preview available now until 25th October that anyone can play.
Listen, I don't need to sell you on the wonderful nature of penguins. Penguins are wicked; everyone loves penguins. A trailer showing a penguin waddling around and honking across town made for an outstanding sight last night. A penguin on a skateboard, pushing around a beachball, and swimming through storms and shipwrecks. Hell yeah, I'm down. My Penguin Friend - a "penguin puzzler" set on an unfamiliar tropical island, according to developer Good Gate Media - is coming to Steam next year, and can be wishlisted now.

item.title: Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux. Read more
item.description:
Epic Games is officially working on bringing its battle royale shooter Fortnite to Linux. The announcement was tucked away at the bottom of Epic's widely mocked blog post revealing the new, "vibe-coded" Epic Games Store, which is also coming to Linux.
At the time, Epic explained it's going to be working with Linux distro maintainers on a set of security requirements needed to run Fortnite. Distros - short for distributions - are operating system variants of Linux, each with its own goals and prioritised system operations. Valve's SteamOS, for instance, is based on Arch Linux. Because of the many discrepancies between Linux distros, each would need to implement Epic's security requirements individually if they want Fortnite to run on their operating system. Fortnite will arrive on Linux via the EGS launcher, but only if a "critical mass of distro maintainers" is reached. Epic didn't specify numbers.
This is big news for several reasons. For one, the move would likely make Fortnite playable on SteamOS PCs and handhelds, including Steam Machine and Steam Deck. Furthermore, even if that "critical mass" is never reached, Epic says its work will be available to other developers interested in bringing their games to Linux.
Perhaps the biggest reason this is a big deal, however, has to do with Easy Anti-Cheat, the Epic-owned anti-cheat service used in Fortnite and dozens of other games - including Dead by Daylight, Rocket League, Apex Legends, and even Elden Ring. While Easy Anti-Cheat does support Linux, including for some of the games just mentioned, many developers choose not to enable it, simply because its "Linux implementation couldn't offer the same level of protection as our Windows implementation," as Epic explained in a separate blog post. This is why many games that use Easy Anti-Cheat aren't playable on Steam Machine or Steam Deck. The post even names Valve specifically, saying the team will "continue its open line of communication" to support Steam hardware devices "to the maximum extent technically possible".
Part of the reason Linux has been a difficult problem for anti-cheat makers to solve is the platform's open nature, meaning certain - required - system-level protections are not guaranteed. On Windows, you can ask users to enable features like TPM 2.0 and Secure Boot, which create that secure environment once hardware requirements are met.
While some of that work can be done on Linux, it requires the interest and participation of distro maintainers. Easy Anti-Cheat plans to use Linux features such as signed kernel, signed kernel modules, and secure boot with attestation to achieve that goal. "These requirements build on work that distribution maintainers already do," explains Epic, "and the more distributions that meet these requirements by default, the fewer players will need to change their setup to play." The goal is to "bring the level of protection much closer to par with Windows".
There is no timeline for any of this at present, but Easy Anti-Cheat will test the announced plans in Fortnite first before making them available to other developers. In other words, if Fortnite gets a release date on Linux, you'll know the work has paid off and we're closer than ever to achieving anti-cheat parity between Windows and Linux.

item.title: The launch of a new live season is hard, and subtle changes to a game can have massive consequences when players get their hands on it. Wardogs proved this true with the launch of its second season this week, as players were able to unlock tanks on day one. Read more
item.description:
The launch of a new live season is hard, and subtle changes to a game can have massive consequences when players get their hands on it. Wardogs proved this true with the launch of its second season this week, as players were able to unlock tanks on day one.
The good news (or bad, depending on whether you feel you've missed out on a head start) is that this exploit has already been fixed. Players could drive just outside of their HQ, drop off pallets, and return to base to earn a sizable amount of XP. This, paired with faster XP gains for the Driver role allowed people to ascend rapidly through the Driver progression track and unlock tanks.
This was a problem, as unlocking anti-tank equipment via other progression paths took far longer than the measly few hours of dedicated grinding these Driver XP exploiters sat through, meaning the vast majority of players were unprepared to deal with the tanks - unless they made use of the exploit themselves and got their own.
In a post made to the Wardogs Discord, Bulkhead co-founder Howard Philpott said: "We're holding our hands up and we got a few things wrong". He went on to explain that a backend update was being pushed through that fixes a progression bug for the driver XP path, stomps out that aforementioned exploit, and also removes the Lonestar (blue team) cash and XP bonuses.
In a video released alongside the Discord, post technical designer Mark Tadros explained that players who were using the exploit "extremely" would be receiving 24 hour bans, though the number of players actually guilty of this falls below the 1,000 mark. Everyone else who partook in the practice, to a less absurd degree, appears to have been left alone.
It's the right call, and in all honestly a tragic result for what otherwise looked to be a direct, laser-targeted set of changes meant to take down some of Wardogs' trickier problems. In the first season, Driver XP was among the most time-consuming to get, so a change to improve that was a great idea. Likewise, the now-removed XP and cash bonus provided to the blue team was a smart solution to that faction, which struggled to win games back in season one.
Even so, the reaction in the community has been mixed. Some, understandably, are a little sad they missed out on the good XP gains. Others noted that this all happened while they were at work - the woe of the employed gaming enthusiast.
Nonetheless, Wardogs continues to prove its merit as a popular and enticing military FPS - and one of the breakout successes of the year. In our early access Wardogs review, we said the game's mix of competitive shooters' best bits with something entirely of its own made it "a brilliantly refreshing take on the genre".

item.title: CD Projekt Red has described its mysterious new game, which is currently known by its codename Hadar, as its "biggest project to date", revealing it's taken "several good years" to reach its current state, and it's still not even in pre-production. Read more
item.description:
CD Projekt Red has described its mysterious new game, which is currently known by its codename Hadar, as its "biggest project to date", revealing it's taken "several good years" to reach its current state, and it's still not even in pre-production.
That's according to CDPR joint-CEO Michał Nowakowski, who told Polish outlet PAP Biznes (translation by DeepL), "At this point we can say that we have a coherent vision of [Hadar's] world and its key elements. The team has started working on the game, although we're not quite at the pre-production stage yet. We're currently developing small prototypes, and we're also testing gameplay elements."
In the four years since its announcement, CDPR has said little about Hadar. However, we do know it won't be based on any existing property, unlike CD Projekt's other major titles - The Witcher having been created by Polish author Andrzej Sapkowski, and Cyberpunk 2077 by TTRPG maker Mike Pondsmith. (Incidentally, I've talked to both Sapkowski and Pondsmith about their work in this regard.)
Earlier this year, Nowakowski shared "an important development update" regarding Hadar's status. "Work on the project is progressing dynamically, and the team has established the foundations of this entirely new IP," Novakowski said in March. "Now, we have clearly defined distinguishing features of this world, and established key pillars that will not only provide the foundation for the game itself, but also, potentially, for other future products." He also mentioned that prototypes were being made in Unreal Engine.
We know from CDPR's most recent financial report in September that there were 33 people working on Hadar as of 31st July, so it's a small project compared to the studio's other titles. 519 people were working on The Witcher 4 at last count, 184 on Cyberpunk 2, and 84 on multiplayer Witcher game Project Sirius. However, Project Sirius was recently hit by layoffs.
Elsewhere in the interview, Nowakowski spoke more about The Witcher 4, which he called "our most ambitious project to date". He also said the studio wanted to "avoid repeating ourselves", so each game should "introduce new narrative and gameplay solutions" as well as "innovations" in main and side quests. "We want players to be confident that when they sit down to play this title, it pushes the boundaries of what an RPG can be and is technologically advanced," he said. The Witcher 4 was recently given a release target of 2028.
He also referenced the recent Remastered update for The Witcher 3, saying the company was "pleased" with sales, which "remain at a higher level than before the remaster", even now the launch discount period has ended. The Witcher 3 broke its Steam concurrent player records after the Remastered edition was released.
Finally, Nowakowski discussed the impact of Sony's decision to phase out PlayStation disc production starting 2028 - putting a possible Witcher 4 physical release in jeopardy. He reiterated much of what he's said before on the matter, saying that because console manufacturers make the discs, there isn't much CDPR can do if they decide to cease production. "A studio doesn't simply decide to release a game and then distribute the physical version itself," he said. "If a particular manufacturer completely shuts down the option to release games on physical media, they simply won't be available."

item.description:
The latest game to pass a 1 million copies sold milestone is Control Resonant. Developer Remedy Entertainment broke the news yesterday, roughly three weeks after the game's release, revealing that Resonant is now the fastest-selling game in the Finnish studio's 31-year history.
Remedy didn't share a digital/physical split, nor say which platform led sales, but these are good numbers for a Remedy game, and even more impressive considering the unusually packed September release schedule Resonant released into.
Remedy CEO Jean-Charles Gaudechon, who took over as boss of the company in February, called this a "very strong start". "Control Resonant is Remedy's first self-published release of this scale, launched into one of the most competitive windows in years alongside the industry's biggest names," Gaudechon said.
"We have always believed Control deserved an even bigger audience, and this launch shows what's possible: we see the game connecting with long-time fans while bringing a significant number of new players into the world of Control, which strengthens its long-term potential."
To that end, Gaudechon said Remedy would continue to build on its two "established" franchises in Control and Alan Wake, adding that: "Our focus is to build on what makes them special, support them, and grow them even further. There is a lot more to come from these worlds."
Although we don't have like-for-like sales data for the original Control, the game sold 2 million copies by the end of 2020, 15 months after launch. Alan Wake 2 - previously the fastest-selling Remedy game - by contrast took about two months to reach the 1 million milestone in 2023. Incidentally, Resonant is the lowest-rated of all three. Alexis Ong awarded it three stars in the Eurogamer review, saying it " feels like it's chasing the hallmarks of a live-service game while trying, only partly successfully, to echo the very deliberate structure and style of the genre storytelling that worked so well in the first game".
Control Resonant joins the likes of The Blood of Dawnwalker, Onimusha: Way of the Sword, Star Wars Zero Company, and Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve as recent releases that have all sold over 1 million copies.
If you're already playing Remedy's latest, or want to do so soon, the Eurogamer Control Resonant walkthrough is a helpful companion that'll make navigating the game's open world and making sense of its many character upgrades a breeze.
